## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai ElevenLabs
creative_generate_image, creative_generate_video, creative_generate_speech, creative_edit_image and creative_transcribe_audio are the core tools. Reach for creative_generate_in_flow only for a modality none of them cover.

Each returns as soon as the generation starts. No view renders here, so poll creative_get_flow_run_status with the returned flow_id and session_ids, waiting poll_after_seconds between calls, until all_completed or has_failures is true, then report the result.

Speech needs a voice_id and a call without one raises: call creative_list_voices, pick one fitting what the user described, or a clear general-purpose one when they gave no hint — never ask — and say which you picked. It only ever comes from that tool or the user, never from memory. To design a brand-new voice instead of picking an existing one, call creative_design_voice with a voice description plus the line to speak and its language — both from the user, never invented — then creative_save_designed_voice to keep the one they pick; creative_list_voices remains how you pick an existing voice.

For a file on the user's own machine, call creative_create_asset_upload with its name, mime type and exact byte size, PUT the bytes to the returned upload_url, then call creative_finalize_asset_upload with that asset_id and the flow_id to get a node_id to pass as connect_from. Never read the file's bytes into the conversation, and never invent a node_id. For a direct https URL, creative_attach_reference_file does all three in one call.

connect_from is required for both creative_edit_image and creative_transcribe_audio — a call with none just raises — so put the file on the flow first. Never say this connector cannot edit images, and never ask the user to attach a file to the chat.

Every generation lands on a flow — an editable canvas the user can open from the returned url. Pass that flow_id back to keep adding to it. When one generation feeds another (lipsync, a voiceover), they must share a flow: call creative_create_flow FIRST and pass its flow_id to every call that follows, since nodes on different flows cannot be connected.

Call creative_get_flow_node_types for the models this workspace can run, creative_get_model_guide before prompting an unfamiliar one, and creative_get_model_schema for a node's effective model_id before passing voice or model parameters to creative_update_node — a guessed name fails validation instead of being coerced.

Generating spends the user's credits. Never repeat a generation call to retry: it starts and charges a second generation. Leave generations_count at its default — several variations to pick from is the point. Confirm with the user only before a long video.

Those variations all live on one node, but a downstream node consumes exactly one, so pin the user's pick: call creative_add_flow_asset_node with that variation's generation_id and wire the node it returns with connect_from or creative_connect_flow_nodes. Read the generation_ids off the run itself, or with a single creative_get_flow_run_status call — it renders nothing, and lists them in the order the view shows them, so "the second image" is the second entry. creative_update_node cannot select a variation and no view reports which one is selected — never say a pick cannot be carried forward, and never ask the user to click in the view to set it.

Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai ElevenLabs
creative_generate_image, creative_generate_video, creative_generate_speech, creative_edit_image and creative_transcribe_audio are the core tools. Reach for creative_generate_in_flow only for a modality none of them cover.

Each returns as soon as the generation starts. No view renders here, so poll creative_get_flow_run_status with the returned flow_id and session_ids, waiting poll_after_seconds between calls, until all_completed or has_failures is true, then report the result.

Speech needs a voice_id and a call without one raises: call creative_list_voices, pick one fitting what the user described, or a clear general-purpose one when they gave no hint — never ask — and say which you picked. It only ever comes from that tool or the user, never from memory. To design a brand-new voice instead of picking an existing one, call creative_design_voice with a voice description plus the line to speak and its language — both from the user, never invented — then creative_save_designed_voice to keep the one they pick; creative_list_voices remains how you pick an existing voice.

For a file on the user's own machine, call creative_create_asset_upload with its name, mime type and exact byte size, PUT the bytes to the returned upload_url, then call creative_finalize_asset_upload with that asset_id and the flow_id to get a node_id to pass as connect_from. Never read the file's bytes into the conversation, and never invent a node_id. For a direct https URL, creative_attach_reference_file does all three in one call.

connect_from is required for both creative_edit_image and creative_transcribe_audio — a call with none just raises — so put the file on the flow first. Never say this connector cannot edit images, and never ask the user to attach a file to the chat.

Every generation lands on a flow — an editable canvas the user can open from the returned url. Pass that flow_id back to keep adding to it. When one generation feeds another (lipsync, a voiceover), they must share a flow: call creative_create_flow FIRST and pass its flow_id to every call that follows, since nodes on different flows cannot be connected.

Call creative_get_flow_node_types for the models this workspace can run, creative_get_model_guide before prompting an unfamiliar one, and creative_get_model_schema for a node's effective model_id before passing voice or model parameters to creative_update_node — a guessed name fails validation instead of being coerced.

Generating spends the user's credits. Never repeat a generation call to retry: it starts and charges a second generation. Leave generations_count at its default — several variations to pick from is the point. Confirm with the user only before a long video.

Those variations all live on one node, but a downstream node consumes exactly one, so pin the user's pick: call creative_add_flow_asset_node with that variation's generation_id and wire the node it returns with connect_from or creative_connect_flow_nodes. Read the generation_ids off the run itself, or with a single creative_get_flow_run_status call — it renders nothing, and lists them in the order the view shows them, so "the second image" is the second entry. creative_update_node cannot select a variation and no view reports which one is selected — never say a pick cannot be carried forward, and never ask the user to click in the view to set it.

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:
       entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X
4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.
5. VERIFY before stopping. Run the most focused relevant test, build, or reproduction available.
   If execution is unavailable, perform a bounded source-level verification and state the limit.
6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:
       entire graph capabilities --json

## When NOT to use the graph

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

## Reference

    locate  ->  entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "..."
    impact  ->  entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X   (one shot: callers, callees, type consumers, data flow, co-change, siblings)
    callers ->  entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in
    change  ->  entire graph diff --base A --head B --json
    detect  ->  entire graph capabilities --json   (inventory-only languages have no relations)
    stats   ->  entire graph stats --repo .        (human-facing token-savings report; not part of your workflow — do not run it unless asked)
- [No Claude attribution in repo](no-claude-attribution-in-repo.md) — no co-author trailers, "generated with" lines, or mentions anywhere in the user's repo

# entire-graph — instructions for coding agents (follow directly)

You have a deterministic local code graph: `entire graph` (functions, classes, methods,
types, routes + call/inheritance relations; no network). These instructions are FOR YOU, the
agent reading this file. Use the graph to narrow exploration without trading away correctness.

## The workflow (mandatory for locate/fix/change tasks)

Your FIRST action on any task that requires finding code must be ONE search:

    entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the task or bug in one sentence>"

Then open the top hit's file with your file-read tool (pass a line range around the reported
line), inspect enough surrounding behavior to justify the change, and make the smallest complete
edit. Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle.

## Hard rules

1. SEARCH FIRST — never grep/find/cat to locate code before you have searched.
2. READ focused source around the result. Widen the check when aliases, generated code, dynamic
   dispatch, or related implementations could matter.
3. Use graph follow-ups only when they answer a real question. For impact or callers, prefer:

4. Make the smallest complete edit and check sibling sites or contracts when the task implies them.
5. VERIFY before stopping. Run the most focused relevant test, build, or reproduction available.

6. Prefer precise queries and line ranges, but never trade resolution for fewer turns.
7. Feature-detect before relying on semantic relations:

If the task already names the exact file and it is small, just read it — the graph saves tokens
by eliminating exploration; when there is nothing to explore, skip it.

1	# VERITAS_PLAN.md
2	
3	**Veritas: Verified changes. Reliable software.**
4	Planning document for neatHack (Oct 10–12, 2026). This file is the first commit after Entire is enabled.
5	
6	**Labels used throughout**
7	- **[Verified]**: read from the official source on Oct 10, 2026.
8	- **[To verify]**: believed true, must be confirmed in Milestone 0 before code depends on it.
9	- **[Assumption]**: our own choice or estimate.
10	
11	**Decisions already made by the owner:** full build as specified (all six views) and this full 31-section plan.
12	
13	---
14	
15	## 1. Executive summary
16	
17	Veritas is an autonomous agent for JavaScript/TypeScript repositories. Given a repo, it finds dependency changes that matter, proves whether each one affects that repo's code, writes a minimal fix in an isolated workspace, recovers when the fix fails its tests, verifies the result, and reports with evidence. Nothing touches the original repo until a human approves; approval opens a pull request.
18	
19	It is built for neatHack's single track ("an agent that completes a substantial task from start to finish") and gives each required sponsor tool a role at both build time and run time:
20	
21	| Tool | Build-time role | Run-time role |
22	|---|---|---|
23	| neatlogs | Find a real problem in a trace, fix it, compare runs | Every model call, tool call, retry and failure is traced |
24	| Entire | Checkpoints for every commit; entire-graph gives the coding agent repo context | Veritas calls `entire graph` commands for impact analysis |
25	| cfo.ai | Business plan: pricing, costs, revenue, runway | Measured cost per investigation (from neatlogs) is the plan's unit cost |
26	
27	Solo build, one EC2 instance, $20 model budget, deadline Oct 12, 11:55 PM IST (planned).
28	
29	## 2. Problem statement
30	
31	Dependency tools tell teams *that* something changed. They rarely say whether the change breaks *this* repository, and they do not prove a fix works. Engineers then spend time on four questions Veritas answers with evidence:
32	
33	1. What changed in the dependency?
34	2. Does it affect this repository?
35	3. What is the safest reasonable fix?
36	4. Can we prove the fix works?
37	
38	Every finding is labelled **confirmed**, **potential**, or **unresolved**. An outdated package is never called a vulnerability unless a published advisory says so.
39	
40	## 3. Target users and personas [Assumption]
41	
42	| Persona | Situation | What they want from Veritas |
43	|---|---|---|
44	| Solo maintainer of an npm-based product | Ignores upgrade alerts because triage is slow | "Tell me which three of these 40 alerts actually break me, with a tested patch." |
45	| Tech lead, 5–30 engineers | Upgrade backlog grows; major bumps get postponed for quarters | Reviewable PRs with proof, so upgrades become routine review work |
46	| Platform / security engineer | Must clear advisories across many repos | Per-repo evidence of real exposure, to prioritise |
47	
48	## 4. Positioning and differentiation
49	
50	Dependabot, Renovate and Snyk are the known tools in this space. Based on their public positioning they open version-bump PRs and raise alerts; Veritas's claim is narrower and checkable:
51	
52	- **Impact proof:** names the files and symbols in *your* repo that use the changed API.
53	- **Verified repair:** a patch is reported as fixed only when the reproducing test fails before and passes after, with no new failures.
54	- **Honest outcomes:** "not affected" and "unresolved" are first-class results.
55	
56	This is the originality argument for judging (10%). The pitch and video lead with "proof, not alerts".
57	
58	## 5. Core user journey
59	
60	1. **Intake:** user gives a GitHub URL (or uploads a zip). Veritas clones into an isolated workspace.
61	2. **Inventory:** reads `package.json` and `package-lock.json`; lists direct and transitive dependencies, installed and latest versions, deprecations.
62	3. **Intelligence:** fetches registry metadata, release notes and advisories; stores each source with URL and retrieval time.
63	4. **Impact analysis:** finds imports and call sites of the affected package; explains why the change matters here.
64	5. **Prioritisation:** scores findings with a documented formula (section 14).
65	6. **Repair planning:** proposes the smallest fix, or "leave unresolved".
66	7. **Isolated patching:** applies the change on a branch in the workspace and runs tests.
67	8. **Recovery:** on failure, reads the test output, revises, retries within limits.
68	9. **Verification:** compares before and after.
69	10. **Report and approval:** user inspects the report and diff; "Approve" opens a pull request.
70	
71	## 6. Functional requirements
72	
73	| ID | Requirement | Focus area |
74	|---|---|---|
75	| F1 | Clone a public GitHub repo or accept a zip upload | Tool use |
76	| F2 | Build dependency inventory from manifest and lockfile | Tool use |
77	| F3 | Fetch registry metadata, releases, advisories; record sources | Tool use, Context |
78	| F4 | Produce a per-finding investigation plan and revise it as evidence arrives | Planning, Iteration |
79	| F5 | Locate usage of an affected package (files, symbols, tests) | Context |
80	| F6 | Score and rank findings with a testable formula | Planning |
81	| F7 | Generate a patch on an isolated branch | Execution |
82	| F8 | Run install and tests in a sandbox | Tool use, Verification |
83	| F9 | On failure, diagnose from real output and retry, max 3 attempts | Recovery, Iteration |
84	| F10 | Journal every step; a killed run resumes without repeating finished steps | State |
85	| F11 | Verify: reproduced before, passes after, no regressions | Verification |
86	| F12 | Report with sources, diff, test logs, attempts, remaining risk | Verification |
87	| F13 | Human approval gate, then open a PR | Safety |
88	| F14 | Trace every run in neatlogs | Required tool |
89	| F15 | Six UI views (section 23) | Demo |
90	
91	## 7. Non-goals and MVP boundaries
92	
93	- JavaScript/TypeScript with npm only. No yarn, pnpm, monorepos, or other languages.
94	- Not a full security scanner. Advisories come from published databases only.
95	- No auto-merge, ever. No writes to the default branch.
96	- Private repos, auth, multi-user and billing are out.
97	- Zip upload is the first thing cut if time runs short (git URL covers the demo).
98	
99	## 8. Technology choices
100	
101	| Area | Choice | Why |
102	|---|---|---|
103	| Language | TypeScript on Node.js 20 | One language for agent, server and UI. Node 20 is pinned on purpose: newer Node can `require()` ES modules, which would hide the ESM-only breakages in the benchmark. [To verify exact behaviour in M0] |
104	| Model access | `openai` npm client pointed at the hackathon LiteLLM endpoint | Free $20 budget; OpenAI-compatible [Verified]. No Bedrock on the AWS account [Verified]. |
105	| Models | `claude-haiku` for development, `claude-sonnet-4.6` for scored runs | Protects the $20 cap. IDs [Verified] on the models page. |
106	| Tracing | `neatlogs` npm package: `init`, `wrapOpenAI`, `span`, `trace`, `flush`, `shutdown` | [Verified] in the TypeScript SDK docs. No auto-instrumentation in TS, so wrappers are explicit. |
107	| State | SQLite via `better-sqlite3` | No managed database is allowed on the AWS account; single file, zero ops. |
108	| Server | Fastify | Small, typed, serves the built UI as static files. |
109	| UI | Vite + React + plain CSS | Fast to build six read-mostly views. |
110	| Sandbox | Docker on the EC2 instance | Isolation for untrusted repo code. |
111	| Tests | Vitest for Veritas itself; each target repo's own test command for verification | |
112	| Code intelligence | `entire graph` CLI, behind an adapter with a fallback | Section 14. |
113	| Host | One EC2 `t3.large`, us-east-1, inside `Hackathon_VPC`, EBS ≤ 50 GB | All [Verified] limits. One instance only. |
114	
115	## 9. System architecture
116	
117	One Node process on one server. The orchestrator is a deterministic state machine; the model makes decisions inside states (planning, impact reasoning, repair) through tool calls. This hybrid is more reliable than a free-running loop and still shows planning and iteration in the trace.
118	
119	- **Orchestrator** (`src/agent`): drives states, enforces limits, writes the journal.
120	- **Tools** (`src/tools`): typed functions, each wrapped in a neatlogs `span({ kind: 'TOOL' })`.
121	- **LLM client** (`src/llm`): the wrapped OpenAI client plus prompts.
122	- **State store** (`src/state`): SQLite.
123	- **Sandbox** (`src/tools/sandbox.ts`): Docker runner.
124	- **Server and UI** (`src/server`, `web/`).
125	- **Bench** (`bench/`): fixed cases, runner, scorer.
126	
127	## 10. Architecture diagram
128	
129	```mermaid
130	flowchart LR
131	  U[User / Web UI] -->|REST| S[Fastify server]
132	  S --> O[Orchestrator state machine]
133	  O --> L[LLM client: wrapOpenAI to LiteLLM]
134	  O --> T[Tool layer]
135	  O <--> DB[(SQLite journal)]
136	  T --> R[npm registry]
137	  T --> A[Advisory sources]
138	  T --> GH[GitHub API]
139	  T --> EG[entire graph CLI]
140	  T --> SB[Docker sandbox: install + tests]
141	  T --> G[git workspace / branch]
142	  O -. spans .-> N[neatlogs]
143	  L -. spans .-> N
144	  S -->|on approval| PR[GitHub pull request]
145	```
146	
147	## 11. Agent execution loop and state machine
148	
149	```mermaid
150	stateDiagram-v2
151	  [*] --> INTAKE
152	  INTAKE --> INVENTORY
153	  INVENTORY --> INTEL
154	  INTEL --> IMPACT
155	  IMPACT --> PRIORITIZE
156	  PRIORITIZE --> PLAN_REPAIR
157	  PLAN_REPAIR --> BASELINE: fixable finding
158	  PLAN_REPAIR --> REPORT: nothing fixable
159	  BASELINE --> PATCH: issue reproduced
160	  BASELINE --> REPORT: not reproduced (potential)
161	  PATCH --> TEST
162	  TEST --> VERIFY: pass
163	  TEST --> DIAGNOSE: fail
164	  DIAGNOSE --> PATCH: attempts < 3
165	  DIAGNOSE --> REPORT: limit reached (unresolved)
166	  VERIFY --> PLAN_REPAIR: next finding
167	  VERIFY --> REPORT: done
168	  REPORT --> AWAITING_APPROVAL
169	  AWAITING_APPROVAL --> PR_OPENED: approved
170	  AWAITING_APPROVAL --> [*]: rejected
171	  PR_OPENED --> [*]
172	```
173	
174	Rules:
175	- Each state is a list of **steps**. A step has an idempotency key (`state + finding + input hash`). Before running, the orchestrator checks the journal; a finished step with the same key is skipped and its stored output reused. This is the State and resume mechanism.
176	- Inside IMPACT, PLAN_REPAIR and DIAGNOSE the model runs a bounded tool-calling loop (max 12 tool calls per step).
177	- DIAGNOSE receives the real test output and the diff of the previous attempt, and must state what it will change and why. That text is stored and shown in the UI.
178	- Limits: 3 repair attempts per finding, 5 minutes per sandbox command, 30 minutes per investigation, a per-investigation token ceiling.
179	- Transient tool errors (HTTP 429/5xx, network) retry with backoff, max 3. Malformed model output is re-requested once with the validation error.

215	## 14. Dependency impact-analysis strategy
216	
217	**Inputs:** the package, the version range crossed, the extracted list of changed or removed APIs from release notes.
218	
219	**Step A, cheap filter (no model):** search the repo for imports or requires of the package. No usage means `not_affected` immediately.
220	
221	**Step B, usage map:** an `ImpactProvider` interface with two implementations:
222	- **`GraphProvider`** shells out to `entire graph`: `search --query`, `impact --symbol`, `neighbors --symbol`. Commands and flags are [Verified] in the CLI reference. Docs describe running them "for automation".
223	- **`FallbackProvider`** uses the TypeScript compiler API to resolve imports and references.
224	
225	`entire graph capabilities --json` is run in M0. **If JavaScript/TypeScript is not supported, the fallback becomes primary** and Entire's runtime role moves to `entire graph diff`/`commit` on Veritas's own patch branch, or is dropped to build-time only. [To verify: language support, Linux install on EC2, whether login or network is needed.]
226	
227	**Step C, reasoning:** the model receives only the changed-API list and the matching call sites (never the whole repo) and returns, per site, "affected / not affected / unsure" with a reason.
228	
229	**Step D, proof:** a finding becomes `confirmed` only when a test or a generated minimal script fails on the new version. Otherwise it stays `potential`.
230	
231	**Priority formula** (unit-tested in `tests/prioritize.test.ts`):
232	
233	`priority = 0.35·severity + 0.30·usage + 0.20·confidence + 0.15·fixAvailable`, each term in 0–1.
234	- severity: advisory severity (critical 1.0, high 0.75, moderate 0.5, low 0.25); breaking change with confirmed failure 0.75; deprecation 0.25.
235	- usage: 0 if unused; else scaled by number of affected sites, capped at 1.
236	- confidence: confirmed 1.0, potential 0.5, unsure 0.25.
237	- fixAvailable: 1 if a fixed version or code change is known.
238	
239	Weights are an [Assumption], documented in the README.

241	## 15. Patch generation and verification strategy
242	
243	1. **Workspace:** clone to `VERITAS_WORKSPACE_DIR/<investigation>/repo`. Create branch `veritas/<finding>`. The user's remote is never pushed to before approval.
244	2. **Baseline:** install at current versions, run the test command, store results. Then bump the dependency and run again. A new failure is the reproduction.
245	3. **Patch:** the model edits files through a constrained `applyEdit(file, oldText, newText)` tool that rejects paths outside the workspace and rejects edits to test files unless the plan justifies it.
246	4. **Test:** install with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in a networked container, then run tests in a container with no network.
247	5. **Verify**, all must hold for status `verified`:
248	   - the reproduction failed before the patch;
249	   - the same tests pass after;
250	   - no test that passed at baseline now fails;
251	   - the diff touches only files named in the repair plan, or the extra files are explained.
252	   Optional cross-check: `entire graph verify` with a recorded baseline [To verify usage].
253	6. **Otherwise** the status is `unresolved`, with the last diagnosis. Generated code alone never counts as success.

318	## 19. Failure-recovery design
319	
320	| Failure | Handling |
321	|---|---|
322	| HTTP error or timeout from a data source | Backoff retry ×3, then mark the source unavailable and continue with lower confidence |
323	| Malformed model output | Validate with a schema; one re-request including the error |
324	| `npm ci` fails | Capture output; DIAGNOSE may change the version choice; counts as an attempt |
325	| Tests fail after a patch | DIAGNOSE reads output and prior diff; new attempt; max 3 |
326	| Sandbox timeout | Kill container; record; counts as an attempt |
327	| Process killed mid-run | On restart, `resume(investigationId)` replays the journal and continues from the first unfinished step |
328	| Attempt limit reached | Finding becomes `unresolved`; branch is kept for inspection; report says so |
329	
330	Each failed attempt is reverted with `git reset --hard` to the pre-attempt commit, so the workspace is never left half-patched.

332	## 20. Security model
333	
334	**Essential for the MVP**
335	- Target repo code runs only inside Docker, never on the host.
336	- Installs use `--ignore-scripts`; tests run with no network, a CPU and memory cap, and a timeout.
337	- Secrets only in environment variables; `.env` is git-ignored; no secrets in traces, logs or evidence.
338	- File-edit and shell tools validate paths against the workspace root.
339	- Original repo is untouched until approval; approval opens a PR, never a push to the default branch.
340	- Bounded retries, time and tokens.
341	- Advisories only from published databases; model-inferred risk is labelled `potential`.
342	- The public UI on EC2 sits behind a single shared access token so strangers cannot spend our model budget.
343	
344	**Deferred**
345	- Per-user auth, private repos, package provenance and signature checks, egress allow-lists, rootless containers, audit log export.

348	
349	**Benchmark set:** `bench/cases/`, 8 small repos created during the hackathon. Each has a `case.yaml` with ground truth: expected verdict, expected affected files, and a held-out acceptance test the agent never sees.
350	
351	Candidate cases [To verify each from the package's release notes and by reproducing in M2]:
352	
353	| # | Case | Type |
354	|---|---|---|
355	| 1 | chalk 4 → 5 (ESM-only) in a CommonJS repo | Breaking |
356	| 2 | node-fetch 2 → 3 (ESM-only) | Breaking |
357	| 3 | marked: default import to named export | Breaking |
358	| 4 | uuid: removed deep imports | Breaking |
359	| 5 | express 4 → 5: removed methods | Breaking |
360	| 6 | A package with a published advisory fixed in a patch release | Advisory |
361	| 7 | Breaking change in an API the repo does not call | Control: expect `not_affected` |
362	| 8 | Outdated package with no breaking change and no advisory | Control: expect no finding |

364	Cases 7 and 8 measure false positives. If a candidate does not reproduce, it is replaced, and the case list in the repo records what was actually used.

366	**Metrics and calculation**
367	
368	| Metric | Calculation |
369	|---|---|
370	| Issues correctly identified | correct verdicts ÷ cases |
371	| Evidence-backed findings | findings with ≥ 1 verified source ÷ findings |
372	| Affected-file accuracy | precision and recall against `case.yaml` |
373	| Repair success rate | cases where the held-out acceptance test passes ÷ fixable cases |
374	| Test completion rate | sandbox runs that finished ÷ sandbox runs |
375	| Recovery rate | cases fixed after ≥ 1 failed attempt ÷ cases with ≥ 1 failed attempt |
376	| Recovery under injected faults | resumed-and-completed ÷ runs killed at a random step (labelled as fault injection) |
377	| False-positive rate | findings on control cases ÷ control cases |
378	| Repeated operations | steps whose idempotency key ran more than once |
379	| Duration | wall time per investigation |
380	| Cost | tokens and cost per investigation from neatlogs |
381	
382	**Fair comparison:** same cases, same model, temperature 0, same limits, both versions tagged in git. Results go to `evidence/bench/<tag>.json` and a comparison table. No improvement is claimed unless the numbers show it; a flat or negative result is reported as such and the next change is tried.

526	| 1:45–2:20 | **Entire.** Architecture: checkpoints plus graph. Implementation: enabled before the first commit. Runtime: Veritas calling `entire graph impact`. Reasoning: why impact needs a code graph. Result: checkpoint list and affected-file accuracy |
527	| 2:20–2:45 | **cfo.ai.** Architecture: measured cost feeds the model. Implementation: the inputs. Runtime: the scenarios. Reasoning: pricing choice. Result: margin, break-even, runway |
528	| 2:45–3:00 | Benchmark table, repo link, close |
529	
530	The script is written in M8 so the UI is built to show these shots.
531	
532	## 29. Business model and financial assumptions
533	
534	Everything here is an [Assumption] and an **input** to cfo.ai. No projection is stated until cfo.ai produces it.
535	
536	- **Model:** subscription per repository, with a free tier for public repos.
537	- **Proposed tiers to test:** Free (public repos, limited investigations per month); Team (per private repo per month); Organisation (volume pricing, priority runs).
538	- **Prices:** to be set in cfo.ai after M7 gives a measured cost per investigation, targeting a healthy gross margin. No price is fixed in this plan.
539	- **Cost drivers:** model inference per investigation (measured), sandbox compute minutes, storage, hosting.
540	- **Usage driver:** investigations per repo per month, estimated from how often dependencies release.
541	- **Scenarios:** conservative, base, optimistic, differing in acquisition rate, conversion and churn.
542	- **Outputs required from cfo.ai:** revenue, costs, gross margin, operating expenses, break-even month, cash runway.
543	
544	## 30. Technical risks and fallbacks
545	
546	| Risk | Fallback |
547	|---|---|
548	| The full scope is large for one person in the time left | Fixed order: agent, benchmark, evidence, then UI views top-down. The agent and evidence are never traded for UI. |
549	| `wrapOpenAI` does not trace through LiteLLM | Manual `trace()` spans around model calls; or move the agent core to Python, where neatlogs auto-instruments |
550	| entire-graph lacks JS/TS support, or cannot install on EC2 | `FallbackProvider` becomes primary; Entire's runtime role shifts as in section 14 |
551	| $20 model budget runs out | Haiku by default; cache model responses by step key during development; scored runs only twice |
552	| A benchmark case does not reproduce | Replace it; 6 cases is the minimum |
553	| First repair always succeeds, leaving no recovery evidence | Use harder cases; never rig a failure |
554	| Docker unavailable on the dev laptop | `VERITAS_SANDBOX=local` for development only; all scored runs on EC2 |
555	| t3.large too small for parallel sandboxes | Run cases sequentially |
556	| cfo.ai will not model without connected accounts | Ask in Discord on day 1; capture whatever it does produce and state the limits honestly |
557	| AWS access ends without notice | Code in GitHub, evidence committed, DB exported after each bench run |
558	| GitHub API rate limits | Authenticated token; cache responses in the journal |
559	
560	## 31. Definition of done
561	
562	- `npm run bench` completes all cases unattended on the EC2 instance.
563	- Each of the eight focus areas is visible in one neatlogs trace of the demo case.
564	- A real failed attempt followed by a successful one exists in a trace and in the UI.
565	- A killed run resumes and finishes without repeating completed steps.
566	- `v0-baseline` and `v1-improved` results are committed with a comparison table.
567	- Six views work for the demo case; Approve opens a PR.
568	- `evidence/` holds neatlogs, Entire, cfo.ai and benchmark evidence, plus post links.
569	- `BUSINESS_PLAN.md` covers pricing, costs, revenue and runway from cfo.ai output.
570	- Video is under 3:00 and covers the 15 required points.
571	- Repo is public, and every commit is dated Oct 10–12.
572	- The quote post is published inside the window.
573

579	2. Confirm the UI cut order in section 23 if the schedule slips.

# VERITAS_PLAN.md

**Veritas: Verified changes. Reliable software.**
Planning document for neatHack (Oct 10–12, 2026). This file is the first commit after Entire is enabled.

**Labels used throughout**
- **[Verified]**: read from the official source on Oct 10, 2026.
- **[To verify]**: believed true, must be confirmed in Milestone 0 before code depends on it.
- **[Assumption]**: our own choice or estimate.

**Decisions already made by the owner:** full build as specified (all six views) and this full 31-section plan.

---

## 1. Executive summary

Veritas is an autonomous agent for JavaScript/TypeScript repositories. Given a repo, it finds dependency changes that matter, proves whether each one affects that repo's code, writes a minimal fix in an isolated workspace, recovers when the fix fails its tests, verifies the result, and reports with evidence. Nothing touches the original repo until a human approves; approval opens a pull request.

It is built for neatHack's single track ("an agent that completes a substantial task from start to finish") and gives each required sponsor tool a role at both build time and run time:

| Tool | Build-time role | Run-time role |
|---|---|---|
| neatlogs | Find a real problem in a trace, fix it, compare runs | Every model call, tool call, retry and failure is traced |
| Entire | Checkpoints for every commit; entire-graph gives the coding agent repo context | Veritas calls `entire graph` commands for impact analysis |
| cfo.ai | Business plan: pricing, costs, revenue, runway | Measured cost per investigation (from neatlogs) is the plan's unit cost |

Solo build, one EC2 instance, $20 model budget, deadline Oct 12, 11:55 PM IST (planned).

## 2. Problem statement

Dependency tools tell teams *that* something changed. They rarely say whether the change breaks *this* repository, and they do not prove a fix works. Engineers then spend time on four questions Veritas answers with evidence:

1. What changed in the dependency?
2. Does it affect this repository?
3. What is the safest reasonable fix?
4. Can we prove the fix works?

Every finding is labelled **confirmed**, **potential**, or **unresolved**. An outdated package is never called a vulnerability unless a published advisory says so.

## 3. Target users and personas [Assumption]

| Persona | Situation | What they want from Veritas |
|---|---|---|
| Solo maintainer of an npm-based product | Ignores upgrade alerts because triage is slow | "Tell me which three of these 40 alerts actually break me, with a tested patch." |
| Tech lead, 5–30 engineers | Upgrade backlog grows; major bumps get postponed for quarters | Reviewable PRs with proof, so upgrades become routine review work |
| Platform / security engineer | Must clear advisories across many repos | Per-repo evidence of real exposure, to prioritise |

## 4. Positioning and differentiation

Dependabot, Renovate and Snyk are the known tools in this space. Based on their public positioning they open version-bump PRs and raise alerts; Veritas's claim is narrower and checkable:

- **Impact proof:** names the files and symbols in *your* repo that use the changed API.
- **Verified repair:** a patch is reported as fixed only when the reproducing test fails before and passes after, with no new failures.
- **Honest outcomes:** "not affected" and "unresolved" are first-class results.

This is the originality argument for judging (10%). The pitch and video lead with "proof, not alerts".

## 5. Core user journey

1. **Intake:** user gives a GitHub URL (or uploads a zip). Veritas clones into an isolated workspace.
2. **Inventory:** reads `package.json` and `package-lock.json`; lists direct and transitive dependencies, installed and latest versions, deprecations.
3. **Intelligence:** fetches registry metadata, release notes and advisories; stores each source with URL and retrieval time.
4. **Impact analysis:** finds imports and call sites of the affected package; explains why the change matters here.
5. **Prioritisation:** scores findings with a documented formula (section 14).
6. **Repair planning:** proposes the smallest fix, or "leave unresolved".
7. **Isolated patching:** applies the change on a branch in the workspace and runs tests.
8. **Recovery:** on failure, reads the test output, revises, retries within limits.
9. **Verification:** compares before and after.
10. **Report and approval:** user inspects the report and diff; "Approve" opens a pull request.

## 6. Functional requirements

| ID | Requirement | Focus area |
|---|---|---|
| F1 | Clone a public GitHub repo or accept a zip upload | Tool use |
| F2 | Build dependency inventory from manifest and lockfile | Tool use |
| F3 | Fetch registry metadata, releases, advisories; record sources | Tool use, Context |
| F4 | Produce a per-finding investigation plan and revise it as evidence arrives | Planning, Iteration |
| F5 | Locate usage of an affected package (files, symbols, tests) | Context |
| F6 | Score and rank findings with a testable formula | Planning |
| F7 | Generate a patch on an isolated branch | Execution |
| F8 | Run install and tests in a sandbox | Tool use, Verification |
| F9 | On failure, diagnose from real output and retry, max 3 attempts | Recovery, Iteration |
| F10 | Journal every step; a killed run resumes without repeating finished steps | State |
| F11 | Verify: reproduced before, passes after, no regressions | Verification |
| F12 | Report with sources, diff, test logs, attempts, remaining risk | Verification |
| F13 | Human approval gate, then open a PR | Safety |
| F14 | Trace every run in neatlogs | Required tool |
| F15 | Six UI views (section 23) | Demo |

## 7. Non-goals and MVP boundaries

- JavaScript/TypeScript with npm only. No yarn, pnpm, monorepos, or other languages.
- Not a full security scanner. Advisories come from published databases only.
- No auto-merge, ever. No writes to the default branch.
- Private repos, auth, multi-user and billing are out.
- Zip upload is the first thing cut if time runs short (git URL covers the demo).

## 8. Technology choices

| Area | Choice | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Language | TypeScript on Node.js 20 | One language for agent, server and UI. Node 20 is pinned on purpose: newer Node can `require()` ES modules, which would hide the ESM-only breakages in the benchmark. [To verify exact behaviour in M0] |
| Model access | `openai` npm client pointed at the hackathon LiteLLM endpoint | Free $20 budget; OpenAI-compatible [Verified]. No Bedrock on the AWS account [Verified]. |
| Models | `claude-haiku` for development, `claude-sonnet-4.6` for scored runs | Protects the $20 cap. IDs [Verified] on the models page. |
| Tracing | `neatlogs` npm package: `init`, `wrapOpenAI`, `span`, `trace`, `flush`, `shutdown` | [Verified] in the TypeScript SDK docs. No auto-instrumentation in TS, so wrappers are explicit. |
| State | SQLite via `better-sqlite3` | No managed database is allowed on the AWS account; single file, zero ops. |
| Server | Fastify | Small, typed, serves the built UI as static files. |
| UI | Vite + React + plain CSS | Fast to build six read-mostly views. |
| Sandbox | Docker on the EC2 instance | Isolation for untrusted repo code. |
| Tests | Vitest for Veritas itself; each target repo's own test command for verification | |
| Code intelligence | `entire graph` CLI, behind an adapter with a fallback | Section 14. |
| Host | One EC2 `t3.large`, us-east-1, inside `Hackathon_VPC`, EBS ≤ 50 GB | All [Verified] limits. One instance only. |

## 9. System architecture

One Node process on one server. The orchestrator is a deterministic state machine; the model makes decisions inside states (planning, impact reasoning, repair) through tool calls. This hybrid is more reliable than a free-running loop and still shows planning and iteration in the trace.

- **Orchestrator** (`src/agent`): drives states, enforces limits, writes the journal.
- **Tools** (`src/tools`): typed functions, each wrapped in a neatlogs `span({ kind: 'TOOL' })`.
- **LLM client** (`src/llm`): the wrapped OpenAI client plus prompts.
- **State store** (`src/state`): SQLite.
- **Sandbox** (`src/tools/sandbox.ts`): Docker runner.
- **Server and UI** (`src/server`, `web/`).
- **Bench** (`bench/`): fixed cases, runner, scorer.

## 10. Architecture diagram

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  U[User / Web UI] -->|REST| S[Fastify server]
  S --> O[Orchestrator state machine]
  O --> L[LLM client: wrapOpenAI to LiteLLM]
  O --> T[Tool layer]
  O <--> DB[(SQLite journal)]
  T --> R[npm registry]
  T --> A[Advisory sources]
  T --> GH[GitHub API]
  T --> EG[entire graph CLI]
  T --> SB[Docker sandbox: install + tests]
  T --> G[git workspace / branch]
  O -. spans .-> N[neatlogs]
  L -. spans .-> N
  S -->|on approval| PR[GitHub pull request]
```

## 11. Agent execution loop and state machine

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> INTAKE
  INTAKE --> INVENTORY
  INVENTORY --> INTEL
  INTEL --> IMPACT
  IMPACT --> PRIORITIZE
  PRIORITIZE --> PLAN_REPAIR
  PLAN_REPAIR --> BASELINE: fixable finding
  PLAN_REPAIR --> REPORT: nothing fixable
  BASELINE --> PATCH: issue reproduced
  BASELINE --> REPORT: not reproduced (potential)
  PATCH --> TEST
  TEST --> VERIFY: pass
  TEST --> DIAGNOSE: fail
  DIAGNOSE --> PATCH: attempts < 3
  DIAGNOSE --> REPORT: limit reached (unresolved)
  VERIFY --> PLAN_REPAIR: next finding
  VERIFY --> REPORT: done
  REPORT --> AWAITING_APPROVAL
  AWAITING_APPROVAL --> PR_OPENED: approved
  AWAITING_APPROVAL --> [*]: rejected
  PR_OPENED --> [*]
```

Rules:
- Each state is a list of **steps**. A step has an idempotency key (`state + finding + input hash`). Before running, the orchestrator checks the journal; a finished step with the same key is skipped and its stored output reused. This is the State and resume mechanism.
- Inside IMPACT, PLAN_REPAIR and DIAGNOSE the model runs a bounded tool-calling loop (max 12 tool calls per step).
- DIAGNOSE receives the real test output and the diff of the previous attempt, and must state what it will change and why. That text is stored and shown in the UI.
- Limits: 3 repair attempts per finding, 5 minutes per sandbox command, 30 minutes per investigation, a per-investigation token ceiling.
- Transient tool errors (HTTP 429/5xx, network) retry with backoff, max 3. Malformed model output is re-requested once with the validation error.

## 12. State persistence and data model

SQLite file at `VERITAS_DB_PATH`. Tables:

| Table | Key columns |
|---|---|
| `investigations` | id, repo_url, commit_sha, status, current_state, started_at, finished_at, neatlogs_trace_ref |
| `steps` | id, investigation_id, state, idem_key, status, input_json, output_json, error, started_at, duration_ms, attempt |
| `dependencies` | investigation_id, name, installed, latest, direct, deprecated |
| `findings` | id, investigation_id, package, kind (breaking / advisory / deprecation), status (confirmed / potential / unresolved / not_affected), severity, confidence, usage_score, priority, rationale |
| `sources` | id, finding_id, url, kind, retrieved_at, excerpt, verified (bool) |
| `affected_sites` | finding_id, file, line, symbol, provider (graph / fallback) |
| `attempts` | id, finding_id, n, plan_text, diff, outcome, diagnosis_text |
| `test_runs` | id, attempt_id (nullable for baseline), command, exit_code, passed, failed, log_path, duration_ms |
| `reports` | investigation_id, markdown, json, verdict |
| `approvals` | investigation_id, decision, decided_at, pr_url |

Large logs are files under the workspace; the table stores paths.

## 13. External APIs and data sources

| Source | Use | Status |
|---|---|---|
| npm registry `https://registry.npmjs.org/<package>` | Versions, `deprecated` field, repository URL | [To verify] response fields in M0 |
| `npm outdated --json`, `npm ls --all --json`, `npm audit --json` | Inventory and advisories for the installed tree | [To verify] output shapes in M0 |
| GitHub REST: releases for a repo | Release notes | [To verify] |
| GitHub Advisory Database (REST global advisories) | Published advisories for npm packages | [To verify] endpoint and filters |
| OSV (`api.osv.dev`) | Second advisory source | [To verify]; optional |
| Package `CHANGELOG.md` from the published tarball or repo | Fallback when releases are empty | [Assumption] |
| LiteLLM `https://litellm.vision.aivar.app/v1` | Models | [Verified] |
| Crustdata | Not used | Optional per rules |

Every stored source records its URL and whether the claim was read from the source (`verified = true`) or inferred by the model (`false`). The report shows them separately.

## 14. Dependency impact-analysis strategy

**Inputs:** the package, the version range crossed, the extracted list of changed or removed APIs from release notes.

**Step A, cheap filter (no model):** search the repo for imports or requires of the package. No usage means `not_affected` immediately.

**Step B, usage map:** an `ImpactProvider` interface with two implementations:
- **`GraphProvider`** shells out to `entire graph`: `search --query`, `impact --symbol`, `neighbors --symbol`. Commands and flags are [Verified] in the CLI reference. Docs describe running them "for automation".
- **`FallbackProvider`** uses the TypeScript compiler API to resolve imports and references.

`entire graph capabilities --json` is run in M0. **If JavaScript/TypeScript is not supported, the fallback becomes primary** and Entire's runtime role moves to `entire graph diff`/`commit` on Veritas's own patch branch, or is dropped to build-time only. [To verify: language support, Linux install on EC2, whether login or network is needed.]

**Step C, reasoning:** the model receives only the changed-API list and the matching call sites (never the whole repo) and returns, per site, "affected / not affected / unsure" with a reason.

**Step D, proof:** a finding becomes `confirmed` only when a test or a generated minimal script fails on the new version. Otherwise it stays `potential`.

**Priority formula** (unit-tested in `tests/prioritize.test.ts`):

`priority = 0.35·severity + 0.30·usage + 0.20·confidence + 0.15·fixAvailable`, each term in 0–1.
- severity: advisory severity (critical 1.0, high 0.75, moderate 0.5, low 0.25); breaking change with confirmed failure 0.75; deprecation 0.25.
- usage: 0 if unused; else scaled by number of affected sites, capped at 1.
- confidence: confirmed 1.0, potential 0.5, unsure 0.25.
- fixAvailable: 1 if a fixed version or code change is known.

Weights are an [Assumption], documented in the README.

## 15. Patch generation and verification strategy

1. **Workspace:** clone to `VERITAS_WORKSPACE_DIR/<investigation>/repo`. Create branch `veritas/<finding>`. The user's remote is never pushed to before approval.
2. **Baseline:** install at current versions, run the test command, store results. Then bump the dependency and run again. A new failure is the reproduction.
3. **Patch:** the model edits files through a constrained `applyEdit(file, oldText, newText)` tool that rejects paths outside the workspace and rejects edits to test files unless the plan justifies it.
4. **Test:** install with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` in a networked container, then run tests in a container with no network.
5. **Verify**, all must hold for status `verified`:
   - the reproduction failed before the patch;
   - the same tests pass after;
   - no test that passed at baseline now fails;
   - the diff touches only files named in the repair plan, or the extra files are explained.
   Optional cross-check: `entire graph verify` with a recorded baseline [To verify usage].
6. **Otherwise** the status is `unresolved`, with the last diagnosis. Generated code alone never counts as success.

## 16. neatlogs integration plan

Docs: https://docs.neatlogs.com/sdk/typescript and https://docs.neatlogs.com/docs/quickstart/wizard

- **Install:** `npm install neatlogs@latest` [Verified]. Try `npx @neatlogs/wizard` first; keep its changes only if they match the manual setup below.
- **Init** (`src/observability/neatlogs.ts`): `await init({ apiKey: process.env.NEATLOGS_API_KEY, workflowName: 'veritas' })`; `await flush(); await shutdown();` on exit [Verified].
- **Model calls:** `wrapOpenAI(new OpenAI({ baseURL, apiKey }))`. [To verify in M0: that traces appear when `baseURL` is the LiteLLM endpoint. The docs do not confirm it. Fallback: wrap each model call in `trace()` and set attributes manually.]
- **Structure:** one `span({ kind: 'WORKFLOW' })` per investigation so all calls nest in one trace; each state a child span; each tool a `span({ kind: 'TOOL', toolName })` [Verified API].
- **Attributes:** investigation id, state, finding, attempt number, outcome, via `activeSpan.setAttribute` [Verified method; attribute names are our own].
- **Errors and retries:** `span()` captures errors [Verified]. Each retry is its own span with an `attempt` attribute. No dedicated retry API is assumed.

**The improvement story (25% + evidence item "the agent improved"):**
1. Run the benchmark at tag `v0-baseline`. Save trace links and screenshots.
2. Read the traces for the worst case and identify one concrete problem (for example repeated tool calls, a wasted retry, oversized context). The problem must be whatever the traces actually show.
3. Change the agent. Run the same benchmark at tag `v1-improved`.
4. Record both in `evidence/bench/` and `evidence/neatlogs/` with the compared numbers.

[To verify: whether a trace link is viewable by people outside our account. Screenshots are accepted either way.]

## 17. Entire integration plan

Docs: https://docs.entire.io/quickstart, https://docs.entire.io/guides/graph/set-up-graph, https://docs.entire.io/cli-reference/graph

**Build time, before any code** [Verified commands]:
```bash
brew install --cask entireio/tap/entire
entire version
git init
entire enable -y --agent claude-code
entire login
entire plugin install graph
entire graph version
entire graph init-agents --repo .
git add .entire/graph-agent.md AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md
git commit -m "Enable entire-graph"
```
- Set `"commit_linking": "always"` in `.entire/settings.json` [Verified] so every commit becomes a checkpoint without a prompt.
- Needs Entire CLI ≥ 0.10.0 and Git ≥ 2.36 [Verified].
- All commits are made from the terminal (GUI clients can skip the hook [Verified]).
- Commit small and often: one checkpoint per commit.
- Entire adds its own `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer to commits and its checkpoints record the coding sessions. That is the required evidence.

**Run time:** section 14.

**Evidence** in `evidence/entire/`: `entire checkpoint list` output, screenshots of checkpoints on entire.io, one captured entire-graph answer from a coding-agent session, one captured `entire graph impact` output from a Veritas run. [To verify: how checkpoints reach entire.io and whether judges can view them.]

## 18. cfo.ai business-planning workflow

Signup: https://cfo.ai/neathacks. A card is required; cancel the subscription immediately in Settings → Billing; the organisers provide credits [Verified]. **Owner action.**

cfo.ai's assistant ("Ari") builds a financial model from inputs [Verified from its site]. It normally connects to real accounts; for a pre-revenue plan we supply assumptions. [To verify: that it accepts typed assumptions without connected data. Do this on day 1, not day 2.]

**Inputs we give it:**
- Product and customer description (sections 2–4).
- Pricing tiers (section 29).
- Measured inference cost per investigation and investigations per repo per month (cost from neatlogs).
- Hosting cost per customer.
- Acquisition assumptions per month, churn.
- Operating expenses, starting cash.
- Request: conservative, base and optimistic scenarios; gross margin; break-even month; runway.

**Evidence to keep** in `evidence/cfo/`: screenshots of the model and each scenario, any export it offers, and the exact prompts we gave. `BUSINESS_PLAN.md` summarises it using only figures that cfo.ai produced, and says which inputs were our assumptions. We do not claim cfo.ai produced anything it did not.

## 19. Failure-recovery design

| Failure | Handling |
|---|---|
| HTTP error or timeout from a data source | Backoff retry ×3, then mark the source unavailable and continue with lower confidence |
| Malformed model output | Validate with a schema; one re-request including the error |
| `npm ci` fails | Capture output; DIAGNOSE may change the version choice; counts as an attempt |
| Tests fail after a patch | DIAGNOSE reads output and prior diff; new attempt; max 3 |
| Sandbox timeout | Kill container; record; counts as an attempt |
| Process killed mid-run | On restart, `resume(investigationId)` replays the journal and continues from the first unfinished step |
| Attempt limit reached | Finding becomes `unresolved`; branch is kept for inspection; report says so |

Each failed attempt is reverted with `git reset --hard` to the pre-attempt commit, so the workspace is never left half-patched.

## 20. Security model

**Essential for the MVP**
- Target repo code runs only inside Docker, never on the host.
- Installs use `--ignore-scripts`; tests run with no network, a CPU and memory cap, and a timeout.
- Secrets only in environment variables; `.env` is git-ignored; no secrets in traces, logs or evidence.
- File-edit and shell tools validate paths against the workspace root.
- Original repo is untouched until approval; approval opens a PR, never a push to the default branch.
- Bounded retries, time and tokens.
- Advisories only from published databases; model-inferred risk is labelled `potential`.
- The public UI on EC2 sits behind a single shared access token so strangers cannot spend our model budget.

**Deferred**
- Per-user auth, private repos, package provenance and signature checks, egress allow-lists, rootless containers, audit log export.

## 21. Evaluation metrics and testing strategy

**Benchmark set:** `bench/cases/`, 8 small repos created during the hackathon. Each has a `case.yaml` with ground truth: expected verdict, expected affected files, and a held-out acceptance test the agent never sees.

Candidate cases [To verify each from the package's release notes and by reproducing in M2]:

| # | Case | Type |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | chalk 4 → 5 (ESM-only) in a CommonJS repo | Breaking |
| 2 | node-fetch 2 → 3 (ESM-only) | Breaking |
| 3 | marked: default import to named export | Breaking |
| 4 | uuid: removed deep imports | Breaking |
| 5 | express 4 → 5: removed methods | Breaking |
| 6 | A package with a published advisory fixed in a patch release | Advisory |
| 7 | Breaking change in an API the repo does not call | Control: expect `not_affected` |
| 8 | Outdated package with no breaking change and no advisory | Control: expect no finding |

Cases 7 and 8 measure false positives. If a candidate does not reproduce, it is replaced, and the case list in the repo records what was actually used.

**Metrics and calculation**

| Metric | Calculation |
|---|---|
| Issues correctly identified | correct verdicts ÷ cases |
| Evidence-backed findings | findings with ≥ 1 verified source ÷ findings |
| Affected-file accuracy | precision and recall against `case.yaml` |
| Repair success rate | cases where the held-out acceptance test passes ÷ fixable cases |
| Test completion rate | sandbox runs that finished ÷ sandbox runs |
| Recovery rate | cases fixed after ≥ 1 failed attempt ÷ cases with ≥ 1 failed attempt |
| Recovery under injected faults | resumed-and-completed ÷ runs killed at a random step (labelled as fault injection) |
| False-positive rate | findings on control cases ÷ control cases |
| Repeated operations | steps whose idempotency key ran more than once |
| Duration | wall time per investigation |
| Cost | tokens and cost per investigation from neatlogs |

**Fair comparison:** same cases, same model, temperature 0, same limits, both versions tagged in git. Results go to `evidence/bench/<tag>.json` and a comparison table. No improvement is claimed unless the numbers show it; a flat or negative result is reported as such and the next change is tried.

**Unit and integration tests (Vitest):** prioritisation formula, journal resume, path validation, manifest parsing, API response parsing against recorded fixtures.

## 22. Reproducible demonstration scenario

Case 1 or 3 (whichever reproduces most cleanly), run live with `npm run demo`:

1. Baseline tests pass on the old version.
2. Veritas detects the major version, reads the release notes, and finds the call sites.
3. It bumps the version; tests fail. **This is a real failure, not a planted one.**
4. First repair attempt; if it fails, DIAGNOSE reads the real output and revises.
5. Verification passes: reproduced before, green after, no regressions.
6. Report and diff shown; approval opens a PR.

Separate, clearly labelled segment: the process is killed mid-run and resumes from the journal.

If the first attempt happens to succeed on the chosen case, we pick a case from the benchmark where it genuinely did not, and say so. We do not rig the agent to fail.

Any simulated package is labelled as simulated in the repo and the UI. None is planned.

## 23. UI structure

Put that line in your message, never inside the file or the piece itself. That line is there so the user can correct you.
- A correction of the audience applies to that piece and to its later revisions, not to other pieces in the session. Treat it as a standing preference only when the user says so (for example "always", "from now on", "remember"), and then save it where you keep the user's other preferences.
- If you are running as a subagent, ignore this section.

## Focus view in this editor
This section applies only while a section titled "Focus mode" appears earlier in this prompt; if there is none, ignore this section. That section describes the terminal's Focus view and does not apply here, and neither does guidance above that text between tool calls may not be shown to the user, or that you should close with a recap that stands on its own. In this editor's Focus view, tool calls, tool results, and thinking are collapsed into expandable summary rows, and every text message you write stays visible in order, including text between tool calls, so the user can see it. Brief updates between tool calls are fine. Do not repeat what you already said in your final message; if the tool calls since your last text message did not change what you said, a brief closing note is enough. Still end each turn with a text message, even a short one, rather than ending on a tool call. If you are running as a subagent, ignore this section. Only your final message is returned to your caller, so put everything it needs there.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type parameter to select which agent type to use. If omitted, the general-purpose agent is used.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).
- Subagents run in the background by default; you'll be notified when one completes. Pass `run_in_background: false` only when your very next action depends on the result and nothing else could usefully happen while it runs — otherwise background it so the user can interject. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.
